questions.topic: Basic concepts and benefits of object-oriented programming
questions.text: What is object-oriented programming? Name its main concepts.
questions.ideal_answer: Object-oriented programming is a programming approach in which a program is organized around objects that combine data and the methods that operate on that data. The main concepts are classes and objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction. Encapsulation hides data inside a class, inheritance lets a class reuse another class, and polymorphism lets the same method behave differently. OOP improves code reuse, modularity and maintainability.

questions.text: What is the JVM in Java?
questions.ideal_answer: JVM stands for Java Virtual Machine. The Java compiler converts source code into bytecode stored in .class files, and the JVM executes this bytecode. The JVM interprets or just-in-time compiles the bytecode into machine code for the specific operating system. Because each platform has its own JVM, the same bytecode runs anywhere, which makes Java platform independent, often described as write once, run anywhere.

questions.topic: Java features and differences from C and C++
questions.text: Give some important differences between Java and C++.
questions.ideal_answer: Java is platform independent because it compiles to bytecode run by the JVM, while C++ compiles to platform-specific machine code. Java does not support explicit pointers, whereas C++ does. Java has automatic garbage collection, while C++ requires manual memory management using delete. Java does not support multiple inheritance of classes, but achieves it through interfaces, while C++ supports multiple inheritance directly. Java also does not support operator overloading or global variables.

questions.topic: Constants, variables, data types and typecasting
questions.text: What is the difference between implicit and explicit typecasting in Java? Give an example.
questions.ideal_answer: Implicit typecasting, also called widening, is done automatically by Java when a smaller type is converted to a larger compatible type, so no data is lost. For example, int i = 10; double d = i; converts int to double automatically. Explicit typecasting, also called narrowing, must be written by the programmer when converting a larger type to a smaller type, using the cast operator. For example, double d = 9.7; int i = (int) d; gives 9, because the decimal part is lost.

questions.topic: Classes, objects, constructors and method overloading
questions.text: What is a constructor in Java and how does constructor overloading work?
questions.ideal_answer: A constructor is a special method with the same name as the class and no return type, which is called automatically when an object is created using new. It is used to initialize the object's fields. If no constructor is written, Java provides a default no-argument constructor. Constructor overloading means defining multiple constructors in the same class with different parameter lists, such as Student() and Student(String name, int roll). The compiler chooses which one to call based on the number and types of arguments passed.

questions.topic: Exception handling: try, catch, throw, throws, finally
questions.text: Explain how try, catch and finally work when dividing a number by zero in Java.
questions.ideal_answer: The risky code, such as int c = a / b where b is zero, is placed inside a try block. When the division by zero occurs, Java throws an ArithmeticException and the remaining statements in the try block are skipped. Control jumps to a matching catch block, such as catch (ArithmeticException e), where we can handle the error, for example by printing a message. The finally block runs whether or not an exception occurred, so it is used for cleanup such as closing files. The program then continues normally instead of terminating.

questions.topic: Java operators, expressions and operator precedence
questions.text: What is the difference between the pre-increment and post-increment operators in Java? Predict the values of a and b after: int a = 5; int b = a++ + ++a;
questions.ideal_answer: The post-increment operator a++ uses the current value of a in the expression and then increases a by 1. The pre-increment operator ++a first increases a by 1 and then uses the new value. In the expression, a++ gives 5 and a becomes 6, then ++a makes a equal to 7 and gives 7. So b = 5 + 7 = 12, and a is 7 at the end. Java evaluates operands from left to right, which makes this result well defined.

questions.topic: Decision making, looping and labelled loops
questions.text: What is a labelled loop in Java? Predict the output of: outer: for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { for (int j = 1; j <= 3; j++) { if (j == 2) continue outer; System.out.println(i + " " + j); } }
questions.ideal_answer: A labelled loop is a loop with a name, written as label followed by a colon, so that break or continue can refer to an outer loop instead of only the innermost loop. A plain continue only skips to the next iteration of the inner loop, but continue outer skips directly to the next iteration of the outer loop. In this code, for each i the inner loop prints j equal to 1, and when j becomes 2 control jumps to the next i. So the output is 1 1, 2 1 and 3 1 on separate lines. Similarly, break outer would exit both loops completely.

questions.topic: User-defined exceptions and multiple catch statements
questions.text: A program has catch (Exception e) written before catch (ArithmeticException e) and it fails to compile. Why, and what is the correct order?
questions.ideal_answer: When there are multiple catch blocks, Java checks them from top to bottom and uses the first matching one. Exception is the superclass of ArithmeticException, so catching Exception first would catch everything, and the ArithmeticException block would become unreachable code. The Java compiler reports an error for unreachable catch blocks. The correct order is to place more specific subclass exceptions first and more general superclass exceptions like Exception last.

questions.text: You created a class in a user-defined package but another class in a different package cannot access its method. What could be wrong?
questions.ideal_answer: First, the class and the method must be declared public, because default access only allows access within the same package, and protected only allows the package plus subclasses. The other class must import the class using an import statement or use its fully qualified name, like mypack.MyClass. The package statement must be the first statement in the source file, and the compiled class must be inside a folder structure matching the package name. Finally, the classpath must include the folder containing the package so the compiler and JVM can find it.

questions.text: You are designing a payment module that must support UPI, card and net banking, with new methods added later. How would you use interfaces or abstract classes in Java, and why?
questions.ideal_answer: I would define an interface such as Payment with a method pay(double amount), and create classes like UpiPayment, CardPayment and NetBankingPayment that implement it. The rest of the code works with the Payment interface type, so the correct implementation is chosen at runtime through polymorphism. Adding a new method, like wallet payment, only requires a new class, without changing existing code, following the open-closed principle. An abstract class can be used if the payment types share common code like logging, since it can hold fields and implemented methods, while interfaces are better for defining a contract and allow a class to implement multiple interfaces.

questions.topic: Arrays, strings, vectors and wrapper classes
questions.text: In a project, a teammate stores a growing list of student records using a fixed-size array. What would you suggest instead and what are the trade-offs between arrays, Vector and ArrayList?
questions.ideal_answer: A fixed-size array cannot grow, so adding more records needs manual copying into a larger array. I would suggest a dynamic collection such as ArrayList or Vector, which resize automatically. Vector is synchronized, so it is thread-safe but slower, while ArrayList is not synchronized and is faster for single-threaded code, so ArrayList is usually preferred today. Collections store only objects, so primitives are stored using wrapper classes like Integer through autoboxing. Arrays are still best when the size is fixed and performance with primitives matters.
